q: Your API gets 1,000 calls a day, and each call runs your code for 100 ms. How long does your code really run in a day, and what does that tell you about an always-on server?
options: About 100 seconds, so an always-on server pays for almost the whole day when nothing runs
About 100 minutes, so an always-on server is well used
About 24 hours, because a server never stops
About 1 second, so serverless is not worth it
why: 1,000 calls times 0.1 seconds is 100 seconds, about 0.12 percent of the 86,400 seconds in a day. A server bills for being on, and serverless bills for the work.

q: A friend says: "Serverless means there are no servers." What is the best answer?
options: Right, the code runs in the browser
Wrong, the code still runs on a machine, but the platform manages it: no patching, sizing or restarts for you
Right, but only on AWS
Wrong, because serverless means you rent one big server
why: Serverless still has servers. You do not manage them. You upload a function, a trigger such as a web request or a timer runs it, and the platform does the rest.

q: The same function gets two requests, one second apart. Which statement is true?
options: Both are cold, because every request starts a new copy
The second is cold, because the first used up the copy
The first is cold because setup code runs first, and the second reuses the copy and is warm
Neither is cold, because a platform always keeps copies ready
why: The first call on a new copy pays the cold start: the platform makes a copy and runs the setup code. Later calls on the same copy skip it. In the lesson model the first call took 500 ms and the second took 100 ms.

q: Nobody calls your function for an hour. What do you pay for that hour, and what happens on the next call?
options: You pay the same as a busy hour, and the next call is warm
You pay nothing, and the next call is cold because the platform removed the idle copy
You pay half, and the next call is warm
You pay nothing, and the next call is warm
why: This is scale to zero: no calls means no copies and no bill. The price is that the next call needs a new copy, so it is cold.

q: A login is saved in a variable inside your function. Later a user is suddenly logged out. What is the most likely cause?
options: The database is down
The next request landed on another copy, or the copy was removed, and a variable in one copy is not shared
The cold start made the variable bigger
Serverless always forgets passwords
why: A function should be stateless. Each copy has its own memory, and the platform can remove a copy at any time. Keep sessions and counters in a database, in a cache such as Redis, or in a token such as a JWT.

q: A burst makes 500 function copies, and each one opens a connection to Postgres. Postgres allows about 100 connections by default. What is the right fix?
options: Add more memory to every function
Put a connection pool between the copies and Postgres
Open the connection inside the handler for each call
Turn off scale to zero
why: Many copies means many connections. A pooler such as PgBouncer shares a few real connections among many callers. Without it, new connections are refused and calls fail.
